Title: The Relationship Between Student Attendance and Achievement, Pre- and Post-COVID
Authors: Tom Swiderski; Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Kevin C. Bastian
NC setting: North Carolina public elementary and middle school students; comparisons through 2023–24.
Findings: More days absent were associated with lower mathematics achievement. The published analysis estimates that restoring pre-pandemic attendance could account for 13–19% of the academic recovery needed in 2023–24.
Practice considerations: Pair attendance recovery with instructional supports; improved attendance alone is unlikely to close learning gaps.
Limitations: First-differences estimates depend on modeling assumptions. The recovery scenario is a modeled projection, not an evaluated attendance intervention.
Remaining question: Which attendance supports improve learning, for which students?
Version note: Uses the 2025 article rather than the different estimates in the November 2024 working paper.

Title: In School, Engaged, on Track? The Effect of the Pandemic on Student Attendance, Course Grades, and Grade Retention in North Carolina
Authors: Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Tom Swiderski; Camille Mikkelsen; Kevin C. Bastian
NC setting: North Carolina public school administrative records before and during the pandemic.
Findings: Attendance, course grades, and grade progression worsened during the pandemic. Disruptions were uneven, with larger difficulties for some middle-grade and historically marginalized student groups.
Practice considerations: Monitor engagement and course progress alongside test scores when targeting recovery supports.
Limitations: Administrative measures and attendance recording changed during disrupted schooling. The study does not identify the effectiveness of a particular recovery program.
Remaining question: Which combinations of academic and engagement supports sustain recovery?
Review basis: Published article and earlier author abstract

Title: Student-Level Attendance Patterns Across Three Post-Pandemic Years
Authors: Tom Swiderski; Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Kevin C. Bastian
NC setting: NC students in grades K–6 at baseline, followed for three years; 2016–19 versus 2021–24.
Findings: The share chronically absent at least once over three years rose from 17% to 38%; persistent chronic absence across all three years rose from 2.4% to 9.6%.
Practice considerations: Distinguish occasional absence from repeated, intensive needs using student histories across years.
Limitations: The sample excludes high school students and requires observation across three years. Descriptive changes do not establish causes.
Remaining question: How should support intensity vary with the persistence of absence?
Version note: First published online February 24, 2025; assigned to a 2026 journal issue.

Title: The Causal Effect of Student Absences Post Pandemic: Evidence from Three School Systems
Authors: Yu Hung Yaow; Seth Gershenson; David Blazar; Ethan Hutt
NC setting: North Carolina, Maryland, and one large urban district; pre- and post-pandemic comparisons.
Findings: Across the study settings, absences remained harmful to test performance after the pandemic, although estimated effects were modestly smaller than before.
Practice considerations: Treat attendance as a continuing learning concern while checking how effects vary by setting.
Limitations: This is a working-paper abstract. Pooled findings are not NC-only estimates; the attainment results described for Maryland should not be transferred to NC.
Remaining question: Do NC effects differ by grade, subject, or type of absence?

Title: School-Based Healthcare and Absenteeism: Evidence from Telemedicine
Authors: Sarah Komisarow; Steven W. Hemelt
NC setting: School telemedicine openings in three rural North Carolina districts.
Findings: Access to school telemedicine was associated with a 2.5 percentage-point reduction in chronic absence and about 0.8 fewer days absent; effects were concentrated among male students.
Practice considerations: Consider healthcare access when investigating local attendance barriers.
Limitations: Three rural districts do not represent every NC context. Clinic access is not the same as an individual student receiving care.
Remaining question: What staffing, costs, and local partnerships support replication?
Version note: Published in Education Finance and Policy 19(2), 252–282 (2024); linked open working paper dates to 2023.

Title: Ending Early Grade Suspensions
Authors: Ezra Karger; Sarah Komisarow
NC setting: Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools; a policy limiting out-of-school suspensions in grades K–2.
Findings: The reform reduced suspension probability by 1.4 percentage points and narrowed the Black–White suspension gap. Average test scores and disciplinary infractions did not worsen.
Practice considerations: Examine alternatives to exclusion alongside classroom outcomes and disciplinary disparities.
Limitations: Findings concern one district and early grades. The working-paper version does not establish effects of every suspension policy or of high-school reforms.
Remaining question: Which implementation supports sustain equitable discipline over time?

Title: Equal Time for Equal Crime? Racial Bias in School Discipline
Authors: Ying Shi; Maria Zhu
NC setting: Statewide North Carolina administrative discipline records.
Findings: Comparisons within incidents and across incidents involving the same students found Black students faced higher suspension probabilities or longer suspensions than comparison students, consistent with racial bias.
Practice considerations: Review disciplinary decisions for comparable incidents, rather than interpreting raw group rates alone.
Limitations: Administrative data cannot observe every behavioral or contextual difference. The study examines disciplinary decisions, not an evaluated remedy.
Remaining question: Which changes to decision routines reduce disparities?

Title: The Effect of Immigration Enforcement on School Engagement: Evidence from 287(g) Programs in North Carolina
Authors: Laura Bellows
NC setting: NC counties approved for 287(g) partnerships compared with counties that applied but were not approved.
Findings: The analysis found lower attendance after program activation, with increases in chronic absence, but no detected achievement effect.
Practice considerations: Investigate community and family barriers when interpreting changes in attendance.
Limitations: The historical policy setting differs from current enforcement contexts. Chronic absence used a 15-day threshold, so rates are not directly comparable with today’s 10% measure.
Remaining question: Which locally appropriate family supports protect school engagement?

Title: What Happens When You Combine High School and College? The Impact of Early Colleges on Postsecondary Performance and Completion
Authors: SERVE Center research team
NC setting: 1,687 applicants to 12 North Carolina early colleges; follow-up through six years after grade 12.
Findings: Lottery-offered students more often earned a postsecondary credential (44.3% versus 33.0%), particularly an associate degree. The overall bachelor’s completion difference at six years was not statistically significant.
Practice considerations: Consider the complete early-college model, including academic and student supports.
Limitations: Results apply to applicants and participating lottery schools. They do not isolate dual-credit coursework from other features of the model.
Remaining question: How do effects transfer to other schools and current student cohorts?
Source locator: Summary pp. 2–5; study sample and methods

Title: CTE-Focused Dual Enrollment: Participation and Outcomes
Authors: Julie A. Edmunds; Fatih Unlu; Brian Phillips; Bryan C. Hutchins; Christine Mulhern
NC setting: North Carolina students participating in CTE dual enrollment in grades 11–12.
Findings: About 9% participated. Participation was positively associated with college credits, high-school graduation, and college enrollment; participation disparities were smaller than in college-transfer dual enrollment.
Practice considerations: Examine CTE dual enrollment as one pathway to broaden college access.
Limitations: Participation was not randomly assigned. The abstract supports associations and does not show that every CTE pathway produces the same benefits.
Remaining question: Which credentials and programs lead to sustained completion and employment?

Title: The Long-Term Effect of North Carolina’s Pre-Kindergarten Program Is Larger in School Districts with Lower Rates of Growth in Academic Achievement
Authors: Robert C. Carr; Tyler W. Watts; Jade M. Jenkins; Yu Bai; Ellen S. Peisner-Feinberg; Clara G. Muschkin; Helen F. Ladd; Kenneth A. Dodge
NC setting: NC birth and education records; pre-K funding exposure and achievement through grade 8.
Findings: Estimated benefits of NC Pre-K funding were larger in districts with slower subsequent achievement growth. Funding benefits also added to the advantages of higher average district achievement.
Practice considerations: Consider early learning and later school environments together.
Limitations: Funding exposure is not individual program attendance. Estimates reflect historical cohorts and rely on the funding-variation design.
Remaining question: How do current pre-K and elementary supports interact?

Title: Effects of North Carolina’s Pre-Kindergarten Program at the End of Kindergarten: Contributions of School-Wide Quality
Authors: Robert C. Carr; Ellen S. Peisner-Feinberg; Rachel Kaplan; Irina L. Mokrova
NC setting: NC Pre-K participants and comparison children followed to the end of kindergarten.
Findings: Average-quality elementary schools showed no reliable overall NC Pre-K effect in this analysis. Language or working-memory benefits were evident under some higher-quality school conditions; literacy and mathematics moderation was not detected.
Practice considerations: Follow several developmental outcomes and the quality of children’s subsequent school environments.
Limitations: Observational comparisons cannot rule out all selection differences. These short-term outcomes and participation measures differ from long-term funding studies.
Remaining question: Which transitions sustain early gains for different children?

Title: Math Acceleration in Elementary School: Access and Effects on Student Outcomes
Authors: Steven W. Hemelt; Matthew A. Lenard
NC setting: Wake County elementary students, 2013–14 through 2017–18.
Findings: Girls were less likely to be nominated and qualify than similarly performing boys. Acceleration effects differed by gender, including evidence of short-term mathematics knowledge decay for girls.
Practice considerations: Review nomination, qualification, and continued participation separately when expanding access.
Limitations: One district’s elementary single-subject acceleration policy is distinct from statewide middle-grade automatic enrollment. The findings should not be treated as universal acceleration effects.
Remaining question: What supports help students remain successful after acceleration?

Title: Objective Course Placement and College Readiness: Evidence from Targeted Middle School Math Acceleration
Authors: Shaun M. Dougherty; Joshua S. Goodman; Darryl V. Hill; Erica G. Litke; Lindsay C. Page
NC setting: Wake County middle-school mathematics placement based on prior test scores.
Findings: Using an objective eligibility threshold increased later advanced mathematics participation for students near the placement cutoff, including students whom discretionary placement could overlook.
Practice considerations: Combine systematic identification with support after students enter accelerated courses.
Limitations: Effects near one district’s threshold may differ for other students and policies. This is not an evaluation of NC’s later statewide automatic-enrollment law.
Remaining question: How do statewide implementation and student supports affect longer-term success?
Version note: Published June 2017; earlier working paper first circulated in 2015.

Title: The Importance of Teaching and Learning Conditions: Influences on Teacher Retention and School Performance in North Carolina
Authors: Barnett Berry; Kevin C. Bastian; Linda Darling-Hammond; Tara Kini
NC setting: 2016 NC Teacher Working Conditions survey, administrative records, and 2018–19 teacher interviews and school visits.
Findings: Leadership, collaboration, planning time, community support, collective practice, and student conduct were positively associated with retention. Associations were often stronger in high-poverty schools.
Practice considerations: Use working-conditions results to structure local conversations and improvement plans.
Limitations: Associations do not establish that changing a survey score causes retention. The study uses an earlier survey and predates the pandemic.
Remaining question: Do these relationships persist across current survey administrations?
Source locator: Exploring Working Conditions; Influences on Teacher Retention
Version note: 2021 brief summarizes a 2019 study; counted as one study family.

Title: 2026 Advanced Teaching Roles Evaluation Report
Authors: Friday Institute evaluation team; authors and contributors listed in the report
Topics: Educator workforce; Working Conditions; Instructional improvement
Design: Mixed methods; school comparison and teacher associations
NC setting: NC Advanced Teaching Roles schools; impact analysis through 2024–25 and implementation evidence from 2025–26.
Findings: The evaluation reports positive schoolwide achievement estimates, strongest in mathematics, but no significant schoolwide turnover effect. Supported-teacher results and release-time patterns were less consistent.
Practice considerations: Specify coaching responsibilities and monitor implementation alongside several outcomes.
Limitations: School comparisons are nonrandomized. The report explicitly describes its two-year teacher-level analyses as correlational, not causal.
Remaining question: Which staffing and coaching arrangements explain variation across cohorts?
Version note: October 1, 2026 report. Prior annual evaluations are related versions, not independent replications.

Title: 2024–25 State of the Teaching Profession and School Administrator Report: NCDPI Findings Summary
Authors: North Carolina Department of Public Instruction
NC setting: NC’s 115 public school districts; employment between March 2024 and March 2025.
Findings: NCDPI reports teacher attrition of 10.11%, compared with 9.88% the previous year. The statutory vacancy measure includes some positions filled by temporarily licensed teachers or rehired retirees.
Practice considerations: Separate departures, movement within the system, and unstaffed positions when planning workforce responses.
Limitations: This record reviews the agency’s public summary, not the full report. Definitions limit comparisons across years and with other states.
Remaining question: Where do persistent local shortages and early-career departures concentrate?
Source locator: March 4, 2026 release; attrition and vacancy definitions

Title: Beyond Prescriptive Reforms: An Examination of North Carolina’s Flexible School Restart Program
Authors: Lam D. Pham; Gage F. Matthews; Timothy A. Drake
NC setting: North Carolina schools participating in the Restart model.
Findings: Restart showed positive mathematics effects, but no detected English language arts or non-test outcome effects. Lower teacher and principal turnover accounted for part of the mathematics estimate.
Practice considerations: Examine how schools use flexibility and retain staff, rather than assuming autonomy alone produces improvement.
Limitations: The comparison design depends on counterfactual assumptions. Results vary across outcomes and do not isolate every component of Restart.
Remaining question: Which local uses of flexibility are most productive?

Title: ESSER III Investments in North Carolina: A Preliminary Analysis of PRC 181 and PRC 182
Authors: Erin W. Manuel; Camille N. Mikkelsen
NC setting: ESSER III applications from 112 traditional LEAs and 177 charter public school units submitted before November 2021.
Findings: Spending plans emphasized technology, personnel, academic recovery, and health and safety. Quantitative and qualitative analyses described differences in planned priorities.
Practice considerations: Use plans to identify investments that need follow-up implementation and outcome evaluation.
Limitations: Plans are not verified expenditures or impacts. This study does not establish returns on ESSER spending or provide evidence about AI tools.
Remaining question: How did actual spending and implementation compare with plans?

Title: Recommendations for North Carolina’s Opportunity Scholarship Program, Pursuant to S.L. 2024-57
Authors: Matthew Pepper; Anna Egalite; Matthew G. Springer
Design: Technical and policy review; stakeholder consultation
NC setting: NC assessment options for third- and eighth-grade Opportunity Scholarship recipients; more than 75 stakeholders consulted.
Findings: The report identifies tradeoffs among comparability, testing burden, and autonomy. Scores from different tests should not be treated as directly comparable across sectors.
Practice considerations: Check test comparability and alignment before making cross-sector performance claims.
Limitations: This is an assessment-design study, not an estimate of the scholarship program’s effect on learning. Recommendations are those of the authors.
Remaining question: What assessment information can be reported validly and feasibly?
Version note: Report dated December 2025; hosted on the Collaboratory site in April 2026.

Title: Project READS NC: Understanding LETRS Implementation
Authors: Paola Pilonieta and Project READS NC team
NC setting: North Carolina teachers and administrators participating in LETRS professional learning.
Findings: The project summary reports knowledge and implementation challenges, including limited preparation time and perceived gaps in administrative support.
Practice considerations: Pair professional learning with protected planning time and support for classroom application.
Limitations: The source presents preliminary survey findings. Perceptions do not establish LETRS effects on student achievement; a final analysis was not reviewed.
Remaining question: How do coaching and implementation supports change instruction and learning?
Date note: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

Title: High-Dosage Tutoring for Learning Recovery in Union County
Authors: Douglas Lauen and research team
NC setting: Fourth-grade mathematics tutoring in nine Union County elementary schools; whole-grade and targeted models.
Findings: The public summary reports preliminary proficiency gains of 8–10 percentage points relative to comparison cohorts, with positive participant feedback.
Practice considerations: Examine scheduling, tutor staffing, participation, and whole-grade versus targeted delivery.
Limitations: The project page does not provide a full technical analysis or uncertainty estimates. Preliminary gains should not be read as a confirmed causal effect or proven return on investment.
Remaining question: Which model is effective and affordable across NC contexts?
Date note: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

Title: Leading Workforce Effectiveness: Inhibiting and Supporting Factors
Authors: Laura Lunsford and research team
NC setting: Eight rural NC LEAs selected from areas with relatively high or low teacher attrition.
Findings: Interviewees described student behavior, leadership turnover, support-service shortages, and local incentives as relevant to teacher retention.
Practice considerations: Explore local organizational conditions and support capacity in retention planning.
Limitations: Purposeful selection and interview accounts do not establish statewide prevalence or causal effects. Findings remain preliminary in the reviewed summary.
Remaining question: Which locally feasible changes improve retention over time?
Date note: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

Title: Mitigating Educator Workforce Impacts Through Coaching
Authors: Anne Cash and research team
NC setting: NC New Teacher Support Program participants and coaches during and after pandemic disruption.
Findings: The summary reports a positive relationship between program participation and retention, together with shifts in coaching time and topics.
Practice considerations: Document the content and intensity of beginning-teacher coaching, not participation alone.
Limitations: Participation may reflect teacher or district differences. The preliminary project page does not supply a full identification strategy or isolate effective coaching components.
Remaining question: Which coaching practices support teachers in different school contexts?
Date note: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

Title: Implementing a Community School Framework in Rural Schools
Authors: Amy Swain and research team
Topics: Family engagement; Student supports; Safety & well-being
NC setting: University-assisted community school work at PW Moore Elementary in Elizabeth City–Pasquotank.
Findings: The project reports increased family engagement, event participation, and staff morale during its initial pilot.
Practice considerations: Use family listening sessions and community partnerships to identify locally relevant supports.
Limitations: The public account is a local preliminary summary without a comparison design. Reported improvements cannot be attributed solely to the community school framework.
Remaining question: Which components transfer to other rural communities?
Date note: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

Title: Keeping Students Safe in the Digital World: School Monitoring Technologies
Authors: Florence Martin and research team
NC setting: North Carolina K–12 school monitoring technologies and stakeholder experiences.
Findings: Participants perceived content filtering more favorably than protection against cyberbullying or self-harm. The summary also reports substantial unmet teacher training needs.
Practice considerations: Evaluate purpose, staff preparation, privacy, and response processes when reviewing monitoring tools.
Limitations: Perceived effectiveness is not demonstrated prevention. The summary does not establish effects of AI-supported instruction or the accuracy of individual monitoring products.
Remaining question: What independent outcome and privacy evidence supports specific uses?
Date note: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

Title: A Study of Cost Adequacy, Distribution, and Alignment of Funding for North Carolina’s K–12 Public Education System
Authors: Jason Willis; Kelsey Krausen; Alex B. Jacobson; Lori Taylor; Ruthie Caparas; Ryan W. Lewis; Karina Jaquet
NC setting: North Carolina’s school funding system as analyzed in 2019.
Findings: The study treats funding adequacy, distribution, and alignment to student needs as connected issues. Authors recommend greater attention to higher-need students, flexibility, and predictable investment.
Practice considerations: Evaluate allocation designs against student needs and local capacity as well as total dollars.
Limitations: The reviewed publisher summary describes an older policy analysis. It is not a current budget estimate, a current legal finding, or a causal evaluation of a proposed formula.
Remaining question: How would current funding options redistribute resources and support outcomes?

Title: The Growing Segmentation of the Charter School Sector in North Carolina
Authors: Helen F. Ladd; Charles T. Clotfelter; John B. Holbein
Design: Longitudinal sector analysis; student fixed effects
NC setting: North Carolina charter and traditional public schools, 1999–2012.
Findings: The study documented increasing sector segmentation and racial imbalance. For the historical period studied, charter schools were not more effective on average than traditional public schools.
Practice considerations: Consider enrollment composition, access, and school variation when interpreting sector averages.
Limitations: Although published within the search window, the data are much older. These findings should not be presented as a current estimate of charter-school performance.
Remaining question: How have access and outcomes changed under more recent policies?

Title: Do Teacher Assistants Improve Student Outcomes? Evidence From School Funding Cutbacks in North Carolina
Authors: Steven W. Hemelt; Helen F. Ladd; Calen R. Clifton
NC setting: NC elementary-school staffing and student records, 2001–2012.
Findings: The analysis finds positive teacher-assistant effects on reading and mathematics, with larger benefits for students of color and students in high-poverty schools.
Practice considerations: Include teacher assistants when considering the mix of staffing investments.
Limitations: Historical funding and staffing variation differs from a modern randomized staffing trial. Current costs, duties, and implementation may change the value of an investment.
Remaining question: Which present-day staffing models produce benefits relative to their costs?

Title: Improving Teacher Retention in Pender County Schools Through a Tiered Model of Support
Authors: Travis E. Lewis; Kevin Taylor; Karen D. Jones
Design: Research–practice partnership; planned surveys and focus groups
NC setting: Pender County Schools and East Carolina University; June 2024–June 2026 project period.
Findings: The September 2025 update reports partnership development, professional-learning design, and piloted instruments. Outcome analysis was forthcoming in that source.
Practice considerations: Connect with the team for updated results and implementation materials.
Limitations: No retention impact findings were reviewed. The stated project period has ended; current completion and publication status need confirmation.
Remaining question: What do the completed analyses show about beginning-teacher retention?

Title: The COVID-19 Pandemic and Patterns of Postsecondary Enrollment in North Carolina
Authors: Daniel Klasik; Matthew G. Springer; Steven W. Hemelt; Sarah Crittenden Fuller
NC setting: NC ninth-grade entry cohorts from 2013–2018 linked with UNC System records.
Findings: The reviewed project page describes questions about applications, financial aid, and college enrollment. It does not report project-specific findings.
Practice considerations: Request the team’s latest brief before drawing conclusions about postsecondary changes.
Limitations: A project description is not evidence of impact. Broad background statements on the page were not treated as results of this project.
Remaining question: Which final findings are available, and for which student groups?
Date note: 2022 award; undated project description. Final publication status requires confirmation.
